## Chapter 2: Anatomy of a Modern Decoder {#sec-ch2}

*The Components Behind Today's LLMs*

### Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- Explain RMSNorm's formula and state precisely what it drops relative
  to LayerNorm.
- Explain RoPE's rotation well enough to say why it encodes *relative*
  rather than absolute position.
- Explain why a gated feed-forward layer needs three weight matrices
  instead of two, and what that costs in parameters.
- For any one of RMSNorm, pre-norm placement, RoPE, SwiGLU, or tied
  embeddings, say whether it is an architectural convention (a common
  but non-forced choice) or something closer to a fundamental
  requirement -- and justify the answer rather than asserting it.

### Why this matters

Chapter 1 gave you the skeleton every decoder shares: a residual
stream, an attention sublayer, a feed-forward sublayer, a causal mask.
If you opened a 2017 Transformer and a 2025-era open-weight model side
by side, the skeleton would look identical -- and almost every detail
*inside* it would be different. This chapter fills in what actually
changed, component by component, and -- just as importantly -- asks of
each one whether it's load-bearing or just a common convention. That
distinction matters practically: a convention is something you could
swap out without breaking the model's ability to function; a
requirement is something the architecture depends on. Confusing the two
is a fast way to either over-explain a trivial implementation choice or
under-explain something that quietly determines a model's memory
footprint.

### Mental model or analogy

This chapter reuses Chapter 1's residual-stream picture rather than
introducing a second, competing analogy -- the "running total on a
receipt" from Chapter 1 still describes exactly what's happening here.
What's new in this chapter is *which specific operation* fills each
slot in that picture (@fig-annotated-block below), not a new mental
model for the stream itself.

### Visual overview

### Technical core

**RMSNorm.** Chapter 1 left `Norm` in @eq-residual-update unspecified.
The original Transformer used LayerNorm, which both re-centers (subtracts
the mean) and re-scales (divides by the standard deviation) a vector,
then applies a learned scale and a learned bias. RMSNorm drops both the
mean-subtraction *and* the learned bias, keeping only a rescale by root-
mean-square magnitude:

$$
\text{RMSNorm}(x) = \frac{x}{\text{RMS}_\epsilon(x)} \odot \gamma, \qquad
\text{RMS}_\epsilon(x) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{d_{\text{model}}}\sum_{k=1}^{d_{\text{model}}} x_k^2 + \epsilon}
$$ {#eq-rmsnorm}

where $x \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}$ is one position's vector,
$\gamma \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}$ is a learned per-dimension
scale, $\odot$ is elementwise multiplication, and $\epsilon$ is a small
fixed constant (not learned) added purely to keep the denominator away
from zero when a vector's RMS magnitude is near zero -- it has no
other role in the formula. *In words:* measure the vector's overall
magnitude (RMS), divide it out so the vector has unit RMS, then let a
learned per-dimension scale stretch or shrink each dimension back.
There is no learned shift and no mean-subtraction step at all.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"RMSNorm and LayerNorm are identical except for naming."** They are
not. RMSNorm drops mean-centering (the $x - \text{mean}(x)$ step) *and*
the learned bias term, not just the bias. Dropping mean-centering is
the more consequential change: it means RMSNorm never asks "is this
vector's average component large or small," only "is this vector's
overall magnitude large or small." Both choices are motivated by the
same practical benefit -- fewer operations per normalization call, at a
cost most current large decoders have judged acceptable -- but "fewer
operations" and "identical except for naming" are very different
claims.
:::

**Where normalization sits.** @eq-residual-update wrote `Norm` as
happening *before* handing the vector to a sublayer -- that placement is
called **pre-norm**. The original Transformer instead normalized
*after* the sublayer's output was added back onto the stream
(**post-norm**). A third option, **sandwich-norm**, applies normalization
in both places around the same sublayer.

| Placement | Where norm sits | Typical motivation |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-norm | Before the sublayer reads the stream | Training stability at large depth: gradients flow through an un-normalized residual path all the way back |
| Post-norm | After the sublayer's output is added to the stream | The original placement; keeps the stream itself bounded, at some training-stability cost as depth grows |
| Sandwich-norm | Both before and after the sublayer | Attempts to recover some of post-norm's boundedness without losing pre-norm's stability |

: Pre-norm vs. post-norm vs. sandwich-norm: what changes is placement, not the normalization formula itself {#tbl-norm-placement}

![The same sublayer and the same residual addition in all three
panels -- only where the norm box sits changes.](figures/rendered/fig-norm-placement.svg){#fig-norm-placement}

::: {.callout-tip title="Working approximation"}
"Pre-norm is more stable to train at depth" is a widely-repeated,
well-supported rule of thumb, not a proof that pre-norm dominates
post-norm on every axis. Pre-norm's stability comes with a
representational-capacity cost as depth grows, which is part of why
sandwich-norm exists at all -- if pre-norm were unconditionally better,
there would be no reason to pay for a second normalization step. Treat
"which placement is best" as a genuine, config-dependent tradeoff, not
a settled question.
:::

**RoPE.** Positional information has to enter the model somewhere,
since attention itself (@eq-attention) treats its inputs as an
unordered set -- nothing in $QK^\top$ depends on token order unless
something makes it depend on order. Rotary position embeddings (RoPE)
inject position by rotating each query and key vector by an angle
proportional to its position, *before* the dot product in
@eq-attention:

$$
q'_m = R_m\, q_m, \qquad k'_n = R_n\, k_n
$$ {#eq-rope}

where $q_m, k_n \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{head}}}$ are a query/key pair
at positions $m$ and $n$, and $R_m$ is a rotation matrix built from
angles $m\theta_1, m\theta_2, \ldots$ that grow with position $m$ (in
practice $d_{\text{head}}$ is split into 2D pairs, each pair rotated at
its own fixed frequency $\theta_j$; @fig-rope-rotation shows one such
pair). The reason this matters: rotating *both* vectors by an amount
tied to their own absolute position leaves the *angle between them* --
and therefore their dot product $q_m'^\top k_n'$ -- dependent only on
the relative offset $m - n$, not on $m$ and $n$ individually.

![Two different absolute-position pairs, (1,0) and (3,2), both with a
relative offset of 1 -- notice the angle traced between the rotated q
and k vectors is the same in both panels.](figures/rendered/fig-rope-rotation.svg){#fig-rope-rotation}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"RoPE adds a learned position vector to every token embedding."** It
does not add anything to the embedding, and it is not learned. RoPE
*rotates* the query and key vectors, inside the attention computation,
by a fixed (not learned) angle that depends on position. The embedding
table from Chapter 1 (@eq-embedding) is untouched -- RoPE's effect is
purely inside @eq-attention, applied fresh at every layer that has
attention, not once at the input.
:::

**Gated feed-forward networks and SwiGLU.** Chapter 1 described the
feed-forward sublayer as "a small two-matrix network," deferred until
now. A plain feed-forward layer is:

$$
\text{FFN}_{\text{plain}}(x) = \sigma(x W_1) W_2
$$ {#eq-plain-ffn}

with $W_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{ff}}}$,
$W_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{ff}} \times d_{\text{model}}}$, and
$\sigma$ an elementwise activation. $d_{\text{ff}}$ (the **expansion
dimension**) is typically several times wider than $d_{\text{model}}$.
A **gated** feed-forward layer, of which SwiGLU is the specific variant
most current open decoders use, adds a second, parallel projection that
gates the first:

$$
\text{SwiGLU}(x) = \big(\text{Swish}(x W_1) \odot (x W_3)\big) W_2
$$ {#eq-swiglu}

with $W_1, W_3 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{ff}}}$
and $W_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{ff}} \times d_{\text{model}}}$ --
**three** weight matrices where the plain version had two. *In words:*
one branch ($W_1$, activated) acts as a gate; a second, purely linear
branch ($W_3$) carries a value; the two are multiplied elementwise
before the shared output projection $W_2$. Nothing here makes the layer
*sparse* the way a mixture-of-experts layer is (Chapter 5) -- every
weight in $W_1$, $W_2$, and $W_3$ is used for every token; SwiGLU is a
different, denser computation per token, not a routing mechanism.

![A plain two-matrix MLP (left) against a gated MLP (right): the extra
matrix creates a second parallel branch that multiplies against the
first, it does not add a third sequential
step.](figures/rendered/fig-gated-mlp.svg){#fig-gated-mlp}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"SwiGLU makes the feed-forward block sparse like an MoE layer."** It
does not. Every parameter in a SwiGLU feed-forward layer participates
in every token's forward pass, exactly like the plain version -- the
only change is *within* one dense computation (an extra multiplicative
branch), not *which* parameters get used. Sparsity, in the sense
Chapter 5 will use the word, means a router activates only a subset of
available parameters per token. SwiGLU has no router and activates
100% of its own weights every time, same as a plain FFN.
:::

**Tied vs. untied embeddings.** The input embedding table $E$ from
@eq-embedding and the output head $W_{\text{out}}$ from @eq-next-token
have transposed shapes ($V \times d_{\text{model}}$ and $d_{\text{model}}
\times V$) -- some models set $W_{\text{out}} = E^\top$ (**tied**
embeddings, one shared table doing both jobs), others learn two
separate matrices (**untied**). Tying halves that specific parameter
cost, at the cost of forcing the same table to serve two different
roles (looking a token up vs. scoring how token-like a hidden vector
is).

::: {.callout-tip title="Implementation-dependent detail"}
Whether a given model ties its embeddings is a genuine implementation
choice that varies across model families, and this workbook does not
have a primary source specifically dedicated to *when* tying is
preferred -- a tracked sourcing gap (see the Build and Version Note).
Treat "tied embeddings" as a real, checkable fact about any
specific model's config -- not as a claim this workbook makes a
historical or performance argument about.
:::

**Convention vs. requirement, applied.** Of everything in this
chapter, RoPE-vs-some-other-positional-scheme and
tied-vs-untied-embeddings are conventions: a model is a well-defined,
functioning decoder either way, and real, current models make both
choices differently. Pre-norm-vs-post-norm is closer to a
requirement-shaped tradeoff at large depth -- it is not free to ignore
once $L$ is large, even though small models tolerate either. RMSNorm
vs. LayerNorm is closest to a pure convention: it changes cost, not
what the model is capable of expressing.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"Every modern decoder uses exactly the same block ordering."** It
does not. This chapter's components (RMSNorm, pre-norm, RoPE, SwiGLU)
describe a common, current combination, not a single mandatory
recipe. Norm placement alone has three real variants in production
models (@tbl-norm-placement); tying is a per-model choice; some models
still use post-norm. "Modern decoder" describes a family of closely
related designs, not one design.
:::

### Worked example

**Parameter cost of gating.** Verified programmatically (see the Build
and Version Note), with $d_{\text{model}} = 8$ and biases excluded from
the count (a stated assumption):

| Design | $d_{\text{ff}}$ | Formula | Parameters |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plain MLP | 32 | $2 \, d_{\text{model}} \, d_{\text{ff}}$ | 512 |
| Gated MLP, same $d_{\text{ff}}$ | 32 | $3 \, d_{\text{model}} \, d_{\text{ff}}$ | 768 (1.5x plain) |
| Gated MLP, compensated $d_{\text{ff}}$ | 21 | $3 \, d_{\text{model}} \, d_{\text{ff}}$ | 504 (0.98x plain) |

: Gating adds a third matrix -- at the same expansion width, that's a flat 1.5x parameter cost, which is exactly why gated models typically shrink $d_{\text{ff}}$ instead of accepting it {#tbl-gated-params}

Holding $d_{\text{ff}}$ fixed, gating is exactly 1.5x the plain design's
parameters, because the formula gains one more $d_{\text{model}} \times
d_{\text{ff}}$ term (3 matrices instead of 2, all the same size). Rather
than accept that 1.5x, many real gated-MLP models shrink $d_{\text{ff}}$
(here, to about $\frac{2}{3}$ of the plain design's width) to land back
near the plain design's total parameter count. Both rows are
*implementation choices* -- nothing about SwiGLU forces either one --
but the 1.5x number is a fixed, checkable consequence of adding a third
same-sized matrix, not a rough estimate.

### Compare and contrast

| Aspect | Learned absolute positional embedding | RoPE |
|---|---|---|
| What it encodes | Each position gets its own learned vector | A rotation angle, applied inside attention, derived from position |
| Extrapolation to longer sequences than trained on | Poor -- positions beyond the trained range have no learned vector at all | Better, though not unlimited -- the rotation formula is defined for any position, but very long offsets still stress the model in practice |
| Parameter cost | One full vector per position, up to a fixed max length | None -- RoPE has no learned parameters of its own |

: Two ways to inject positional information, compared on what they cost and how they behave outside the training distribution {#tbl-positional}

### Applied exercise

Here is a (fictional, illustrative) model config excerpt:

```
hidden_size: 2048
num_attention_heads: 16
intermediate_size: 5504
hidden_act: "silu"
rms_norm_eps: 1e-5
tie_word_embeddings: false
rope_theta: 10000.0
```

From this excerpt alone: (a) which normalization scheme does this model
use, and how do you know from a field name alone versus what you'd need
to check the model's own code to be sure? (b) does it use a gated
feed-forward layer -- what field is the giveaway? (c) is
`intermediate_size` closer to $4 \times$ `hidden_size` (a plain-MLP-style
ratio) or closer to $\frac{2}{3} \times 4 \times$ `hidden_size` (a
gated, compensated ratio, per this chapter's worked example)? (d) are
embeddings tied? Write your reasoning for each, not just the answer --
this is the same skill Chapter 6's case studies will ask of you at
real-model scale.

### Interview lens

*"Why does this model use RoPE instead of learned positional
embeddings?"* A strong answer states RoPE's relative-position property
(@eq-rope) as the mechanism, names at least one concrete consequence
(no learned positional parameters; different, generally better
long-context extrapolation behavior than a learned table with a fixed
max length), and resists the temptation to just say "it's more modern"
without saying what specifically changed. *"Walk me through what
SwiGLU changes about the MLP"* is answered well by describing the extra
parallel branch and the elementwise multiply (@eq-swiglu), explicitly
including the 1.5x-or-compensated parameter tradeoff from this
chapter's worked example -- an answer that skips the parameter cost
entirely is incomplete for a systems-flavored interview.

### Chapter recap

- RMSNorm drops both mean-centering and the learned bias LayerNorm has,
  keeping only a magnitude rescale (plus a small fixed $\epsilon$ to
  avoid dividing by zero).
- Pre-norm, post-norm, and sandwich-norm describe *where* normalization
  sits relative to a sublayer and the residual add -- not three
  different normalization formulas.
- RoPE rotates queries and keys by a position-dependent angle inside
  attention, so their dot product depends only on relative offset --
  it adds nothing to the embedding table and learns nothing.
- A gated (SwiGLU-style) feed-forward layer adds one parallel matrix
  and one elementwise multiply; at matched expansion width that's a
  flat 1.5x parameter cost, which is why real models often shrink the
  expansion width to compensate.
- Tied vs. untied embeddings and RoPE-vs-alternative are conventions;
  norm placement is closer to a real training-stability tradeoff at
  depth. None of this chapter's components is used identically by
  every current model.
